L14: # Soft Tissue Sarcoma Treatment (PDQ®)–Health Professional Version
L15: ## General Information About Soft Tissue Sarcoma
L16: 
L17: 【8†Go to Patient Version】
L18: ### Incidence and Mortality
L19: 
L20: Estimated new cases and deaths from soft tissue sarcoma in the United States in 2025:[【9†1】]
L21: 
L22:   * New cases: 13,520.
L23:   * Deaths: 5,410.
L24: The reported international incidence of soft tissue sarcoma ranges from 1.8 to 5 cases per 100,000 individuals per year.[【10†2】] The rate of new cases of soft tissue cancer in the United States was 3.4 per 100,000 people per year based on age-adjusted cases from 2017 to 2021. The death rate was 1.3 per 100,000 people per year based on age-adjusted deaths from 2018 to 2022.[【11†3】]
L25: ### Risk Factors
L26: 
L27: Most soft tissue sarcomas are sporadic. Risk factors include:[【12†4】-【13†6】]
L28: 
L29:   * Previous radiation therapy.
L30:   * Chronic lymphedema (risk factor for lymphangiosarcoma).
L31:   * Exposure to the chemicals thorium dioxide (Thorotrast), vinyl chloride, or arsenic. These are established carcinogens for hepatic angiosarcomas.
L32:   * HIV and human herpesvirus 8 infection. These viruses have been implicated in the pathogenesis of Kaposi sarcoma. For more information, see 【14†Kaposi Sarcoma Treatment】.
L33: Soft tissue sarcomas occur more frequently in patients with the following inherited syndromes:[【12†4】-【13†6】]
L34:   * Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53 pathogenic variant).
L35:   * von Recklinghausen disease (neurofibromatosis type 1; NF1 pathogenic variant).
L36:   * Gardner syndrome (APC pathogenic variant).
L37:   * Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome; PTCH1 pathogenic variant).
L38:   * Tuberous sclerosis (Bourneville disease; TSC1 or TSC2 pathogenic variant).
L39:   * Werner syndrome (adult progeria; WRN pathogenic variant).
L40: ### Clinical Features
L41: 
L42: Soft tissue sarcomas are a heterogenous family of malignant tumors that may arise in nearly any organ system. The anatomical distribution in adults is as follows:[【15†5】]
L43: 
L44:   * Extremities (45%).
L45:   * Intra-abdominal organs (38%).
L46:   * Trunk (10%).
L47:   * Head and neck (5%).
L48: ### Diagnostic Evaluation
L49: Adequate tissue should be obtained via either image-guided core-needle biopsy or planned incisional biopsy (for select cases). The samples should be reviewed by a pathologist who is experienced in diagnosing sarcomas. Careful planning of the initial biopsy, with consultation among the surgeon, radiation oncologist, and interventional radiologist, is important to avoid compromising subsequent curative resection.
L50: In general, incisional biopsies are reserved for patients whose prior core-needle biopsies were nondiagnostic or when a core-needle biopsy cannot be safely performed because of anatomical constraints.
L51: Before any intervention is initiated, imaging is performed to evaluate the sarcoma and determine if there are metastases. The following modalities may be used as clinically indicated:
L52:   * Plain radiography.
L53:   * Computed tomography (CT).
L54:   * Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
L55:   * Positron emission tomography (PET) scan and bone scan. May be used along with CT. PET imaging is particularly useful for sarcoma subtypes with a propensity for lymph node metastases (e.g., synovial sarcoma, clear cell sarcoma, angiosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and epithelioid sarcoma).
L56: ### Prognostic Factors
L57: 
L58: Poor prognostic factors in adults with soft tissue sarcomas include:[【12†4】-【16†15】]
L59: 
L60:   * Age older than 60 years.
L61:   * Tumor size (e.g., larger than 5 cm in greatest dimension, variable impact depending on sarcoma subtype).
L62:   * High histological grade of the tumor (incorporating histology-specific differentiation, mitotic rate, and extent of tumor necrosis).
L63:   * Advanced pathological stage of the tumor at the time of diagnosis.
L64:   * Positive tumor margins after surgery.[【17†10】]
L65: Small low-grade tumors, particularly in the trunk or extremities, are frequently curable by surgery alone. Higher-grade sarcomas are associated with higher local-treatment failure rates and increased metastatic potential.[【18†16】]
L66: 
L67: Prognostic nomograms (incorporating specific variables) have been developed for soft tissue sarcomas of the retroperitoneum and the extremities.[【19†11】-【20†14】]
L68: ### Follow-Up Testing
L69: 
L70: PET and CT imaging may have higher sensitivity than contrast-enhanced CT imaging when recurrent sarcoma is suspected. Late recurrences (more than 5 years from initial diagnosis) are seen with some histologies, such as synovial sarcoma or alveolar soft-part sarcoma.[【21†17】,【22†18】]
L71: 
L72: Evidence (posttreatment imaging surveillance):
L73:   1. A retrospective review included 174 consecutive patients with soft tissue sarcoma of the limb who underwent follow-up by oncologists at a single center from 2003 to 2009.[【23†19】][【24†Level of evidence C2】] The rate and site of recurrence and mode of detection were analyzed. The following results were reported:
L74:     1. Eighty-two patients (47%) experienced relapse.
L75:     2. Isolated local recurrences occurred in 26 patients, and local relapse with synchronous pulmonary metastases occurred in 5 patients.
L76: 
L77:        * Local recurrences were detected clinically in 30 of the 31 patients.
L78:        * MRI identified only one local recurrence.
L79: 
L80:     3. Twenty-eight patients (16%) developed isolated lung metastases.
L81:        * The lung metastases were amenable to resections in nine patients, seven of whom were free of disease after treatment.
L82:        * Lung metastases were detected by chest x-ray in 19 patients, by CT scan in 3 patients, and clinically in 11 patients.
L83: 
L84:     4. Twenty-three patients developed nonpulmonary metastases.
L85:     5. More than 80% of the relapses occurred in the first 2 years of follow-up. Later recurrences were also observed.
L86: This study supports imaging surveillance for detection of lung metastases. Local recurrences at the primary site were usually detected by clinical examination. The impact of metastases detection on overall survival or quality of life is unknown.[【23†19】]

L12: # Desmoid Tumor
L13: ## What is desmoid tumor?
L14: 
L15: 【6†Participate in Our Trial You can help speed up the development of new treatments by giving researchers the tools they need.】
L16: Desmoid tumors grow from the connective tissue in your body. They grow from 【7†fibroblast】 cells, which make up connective tissue and are also important for wound healing. Connective tissue supports and connects your bones, ligaments, and muscles, and helps hold your organs in place. Desmoid tumors are also known as aggressive fibromatosis or desmoid-type fibromatosis.
L17: A desmoid tumor can occur anywhere in the body since connective tissue is found everywhere in your body. Desmoid tumors are often found in the abdomen, as well as the shoulders, upper arms, and thighs.
L18: Desmoid tumors are locally aggressive tumors. While the cells of the desmoid tumor do not travel to other parts of the body like cancer can, they can invade nearby tissue and are often very painful. Desmoid tumors can grow slowly or very quickly. The quicker they grow the more serious they are. Desmoid tumors can be difficult to completely remove with surgery.
L19: 
L20: Desmoid tumors are most common in people between the ages of 15 and 60 years. They are more common in females than males.
L21: ## How common is desmoid tumor?
L22: 
L23: For every one million people worldwide, two to four are diagnosed with a desmoid tumor per year.
L24: ## How is desmoid tumor diagnosed?
L25: 
L26: Some people with desmoid tumors have symptoms, while others do not. Symptoms can include pain, swelling in the area of the tumor, sleep loss, or difficulty moving. For people without symptoms, these tumors can be discovered if the person has an imaging test for another reason.
L27: 
L28: Imaging: If you have symptoms of a desmoid tumor, your doctor may use imaging scans such as CT, MRI, or ultrasound to see where the tumor is and its size.
L29: Biopsy: To check if the tumor is a desmoid tumor your doctor will do a biopsy, taking a small amount of the tumor out with a needle. A pathologist will study the cells under the microscope to see what kind of tumor it is. Depending on the tumor's location, it may be difficult for the doctor to take a biopsy.
L30: ## How is desmoid tumor treated?
L31: 
L32: Treatment for each patient will be unique so you should go to an expert in sarcoma treatment to decide the best approach for your tumor.
L33: 
L34: Desmoid tumors can be hard to predict. They can shrink and go away on their own, they can remain the same size, or they can grow quickly.
L35: 
L36: Treatment options to discuss with your doctor include:
L37: Watch and wait: In some cases, the tumor grows very slowly, or even shrinks without any treatment. It may be safest for your doctor to check your tumor regularly without treating it.
L38: 
L39: Surgery: Surgery has been a standard treatment for desmoid tumors in the past but this may be changing. Given that the tumor often returns to the same location after surgery, doctors are looking for other treatment options.
L40: Radiation therapy: Radiation therapy is a treatment option for some desmoid tumors. Given that radiation therapy can cause other cancers in the future, it is important to discuss alternatives with your doctor.
L41: 
L42: Chemotherapy: There is no standard chemotherapy for desmoid tumors but promising new drugs have been shown to shrink these tumors.
L43: 
L44: It is important to discuss these different options with your doctor and seek second opinions, if possible.
L45: ## Do desmoid tumors run in families?
L46: 
L47: In 5% to 10% of cases, desmoid tumors may run in families. Those diagnosed with 【8†Gardner syndrome†rarediseases.info.nih.gov】, a rare syndrome that also runs in families, have a high risk of colorectal cancer and desmoid tumor.
L48: ## How does desmoid tumor form?
L49: 
L50: Scientists are always working to understand how tumors form but it can be hard to prove. We know that some people with a family history of desmoid tumors have a change in a gene called adenomatous polyposis coli, or APC. This change causes too much of a protein called beta-catenin in parts of your cells. Too much beta-catenin can cause cells to grow when they shouldn’t. In some desmoid tumors, there is too much beta-catenin, even though APC is normal.
L51: APC and beta-catenin are important in many common cancers, such as colon cancer, and scientists are trying to use this information to develop better cancer treatments, which will help people with desmoid tumors.
L52: ## What is the prognosis for someone with a desmoid tumor?
L53: 
L54: The estimate of how a disease will affect you long-term is called prognosis. Every person is different and prognosis will depend on many factors, such as:
L55: 
L56:   * Where the tumor is in your body
L57:   * How fast the tumor grows
L58:   * How much of the tumor was taken out during surgery
L59: 
L60: If you want information on your prognosis, it is important to talk to your doctor. NCI also has 【9†resources to help you understand cancer prognosis】.
L61: Doctors estimate desmoid tumor survival rates by how groups of people with desmoid tumors have done in the past. Given that there are so few desmoid tumor patients, survival rates may not be very accurate. They also don’t consider newer treatments being developed.
L62: Most desmoid tumors do not impact lifespan but they are very difficult to get rid of and can be painful to live with. Desmoid tumors growing in the abdomen can cause problems, such as blocking your intestines. It is important that your doctor monitor the growth of these tumors carefully.

L256: ## Treatment Option Overview for Soft Tissue Sarcoma
L257: ### Planning Therapy
L258: Complete staging and treatment planning by a multidisciplinary team of cancer specialists is required to determine the optimal treatment for patients with soft tissue sarcoma. In most cases, a combined modality approach of preoperative radiation therapy (preRT) or postoperative radiation therapy (PORT) is used for treatment, rather than a radical surgical procedure such as amputation. Surgery without PORT may be possible in selected cases. The role of chemotherapy is not well defined.

L542: ## Treatment of Stage I Soft Tissue Sarcoma
L543: ### Treatment Options for Stage I Soft Tissue Sarcoma
L544: 
L545: Treatment options for 【67†stage I soft tissue sarcoma】 include:
L546: 
L547:   1. 【68†Surgery】.
L548:   2. 【69†Surgery with radiation therapy】.
L549:   3. 【70†High-dose radiation therapy】.
L550: 
L551: For more information on 【209†surgery】 and 【89†radiation therapy】, see the 【210†Treatment Option Overview for Soft Tissue Sarcoma】 section.
L552: Because of the low metastatic potential of these tumors, chemotherapy is usually not given to patients with stage I soft tissue sarcoma.[【211†1】,【212†2】]
L553: #### Surgery
L554: 
L555: Low-grade soft tissue sarcomas have little metastatic potential, but they have a tendency to recur locally. The treatment of choice for patients with early-stage sarcomas (tumors ≤5 cm in diameters) is surgical excision with negative tissue margins (of 1 cm to 2 cm or larger) in all directions.[【213†3】-【214†10】]

L793: ## Treatment of Recurrent Soft Tissue Sarcoma
L794: 
L795: Treatment of patients with recurrent soft tissue sarcoma depends on the clinical presentation of the disease and previous treatment.
L815: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved eribulin, trabectedin, and pazopanib for the treatment of soft tissue sarcomas after failure of a first-line chemotherapy regimen.
L824: ##### Trabectedin
L825: 
L826: Trabectedin is an FDA-approved option for second-line treatment of patients with advanced liposarcoma and leiomyosarcoma.
L827: 
L828: Evidence (trabectedin):
L829: 
L830:   1. The approval of trabectedin was based on a phase III randomized study (NCT01343277) of 518 patients who received trabectedin (1.5 mg/m 2 over 24 hours on day 1 every 21 days) or dacarbazine (1,000 mg/m 2 on day 1 every 21 days).[19]
L841:   1. The phase III, randomized, double-blind PALETTE study (NCT00753688) from the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer compared pazopanib (800 mg daily) with placebo in 369 patients with different soft tissue sarcoma subtypes, excluding adipocytic sarcomas and gastrointestinal stromal tumors. Patients were enrolled after disease progression on a first-line anthracycline-based regimen.[21]
L847: Based on these data, pazopanib was approved by the FDA in 2012 for the treatment of patients with soft tissue sarcomas (except the adipocytic subtypes) who have received previous chemotherapy.
L848: 
L849: After first-line chemotherapy, other agents can be considered, including:
L850: 
L851:   * Ifosfamide with or without etoposide.
L852:   * Dacarbazine.
L853:   * Temozolomide.
L854:   * Vinorelbine.
L855:   * Regorafenib.
L869:   2. The phase II Alliance A091401 study (NCT02500797) randomly assigned patients to receive nivolumab (n = 43) versus nivolumab and ipilimumab (n = 42) for the treatment of different soft tissue sarcomas.[23]

L14: # Palliative Care in Cancer
L15: ##
L16: 
L17: What is palliative care?
L18: Palliative care is care meant to improve the 【8†quality of life】 of patients who have a serious or life-threatening disease, such as cancer. It can be given with or without curative care. Palliative care is an approach to care that addresses the person as a whole, not just their disease.
L19: The goal is to prevent or treat, as early as possible, the symptoms and 【9†side effects】 of the disease and its treatment, in addition to any related psychological, social, and spiritual problems.  Patients may receive palliative care in the hospital, an outpatient clinic, a long-term care facility, or at home under the direction of a licensed health care provider. Anyone can receive palliative care regardless of their age or stage of disease.

L542: ## Treatment of Stage I Soft Tissue Sarcoma
L553: #### Surgery
L554: 
L555: Low-grade soft tissue sarcomas have little metastatic potential, but they have a tendency to recur locally. The treatment of choice for patients with early-stage sarcomas (tumors ≤5 cm in diameters) is surgical excision with negative tissue margins (of 1 cm to 2 cm or larger) in all directions.[【213†3】-【214†10】]

L740: ##### Treatment of desmoid tumors
L741: 
L742: Evidence (nirogacestat vs. placebo):
L743:   1. A phase III placebo-controlled trial (NCT03785964) included adults with progressing desmoid tumors who had either not received prior therapy or whose disease was refractory to prior therapy. Patients were stratified according to tumor location (intra-abdominal vs. extra-abdominal). Patients were randomly assigned to receive either oral nirogacestat (150 mg twice daily) or placebo (twice daily).
L744: A total of 142 patients were assigned (70 to the nirogacestat group and 72 to the placebo group) across 37 sites in the United States, Canada, and Europe. Thirty-seven patients in each group were women of childbearing potential. A total of 110 patients (77%) had previously undergone systemic therapy, radiation therapy, or surgery. The median follow-up was 15.9 months.[28]
L745:     1. The median PFS could not be estimated in the nirogacestat group (due to a low number of events) and was 15.1 months in the placebo group. The risk of disease progression or death was 71% lower in the nirogacestat group (HR, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.15–0.55; P < .001).[28][【106†Level of evidence B1】]
L746:     2. The objective response rate was 41% in the nirogacestat group and 8% in the placebo group (P < .001). Complete responses occurred in 7% of patients in the nirogacestat group and 0% of patients in the placebo group.
L747:     3. Several patient-reported outcome measures were collected and assessed, including:
L748:        * Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form.
L749:        * GOunder/Desmoid Tumor Research Foundation DEsmoid Symptom/Impact Scale (GODDESS) (comprising the Desmoid Tumor Impact Scale physical functioning domain score and the Desmoid Tumor Symptom Scale).
L750:        * European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire (EORTC QLQ-C30) scales for global health status-quality of life, physical functioning, and role functioning.

L793: ## Treatment of Recurrent Soft Tissue Sarcoma
L794: 
L795: Treatment of patients with recurrent soft tissue sarcoma depends on the clinical presentation of the disease and previous treatment.
L796: ### Treatment Options for Recurrent Soft Tissue Sarcoma
L797: 
L798: Treatment options for recurrent soft tissue sarcoma include:
L799: 
L800:   1. 【80†Surgery with or without radiation therapy】.
L801:   2. 【81†Chemotherapy and targeted therapy】.
L802: 
L803:      * Eribulin.
L804:      * Trabectedin.
L805:      * Pazopanib.
L806: 
L807:   3. 【82†Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy】.
L808: 
L809: For more information on 【209†surgery】, 【89†radiation therapy】, and 【227†chemotherapy】, see the 【210†Treatment Option Overview for Soft Tissue Sarcoma】 section.
L815: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved eribulin, trabectedin, and pazopanib for the treatment of soft tissue sarcomas after failure of a first-line chemotherapy regimen.
L824: ##### Trabectedin
L825: 
L826: Trabectedin is an FDA-approved option for second-line treatment of patients with advanced liposarcoma and leiomyosarcoma.
L827: 
L828: Evidence (trabectedin):
L829: 
L830:   1. The approval of trabectedin was based on a phase III randomized study (NCT01343277) of 518 patients who received trabectedin (1.5 mg/m 2 over 24 hours on day 1 every 21 days) or dacarbazine (1,000 mg/m 2 on day 1 every 21 days).[19]
L841:   1. The phase III, randomized, double-blind PALETTE study (NCT00753688) from the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer compared pazopanib (800 mg daily) with placebo in 369 patients with different soft tissue sarcoma subtypes, excluding adipocytic sarcomas and gastrointestinal stromal tumors. Patients were enrolled after disease progression on a first-line anthracycline-based regimen.[21]
L847: Based on these data, pazopanib was approved by the FDA in 2012 for the treatment of patients with soft tissue sarcomas (except the adipocytic subtypes) who have received previous chemotherapy.
L848: 
L849: After first-line chemotherapy, other agents can be considered, including:
L850: 
L851:   * Ifosfamide with or without etoposide.
L852:   * Dacarbazine.
L853:   * Temozolomide.
L854:   * Vinorelbine.
L855:   * Regorafenib.
L869:   2. The phase II Alliance A091401 study (NCT02500797) randomly assigned patients to receive nivolumab (n = 43) versus nivolumab and ipilimumab (n = 42) for the treatment of different soft tissue sarcomas.[23]
